item.title: Reversible Atlantic overturning despite continued Greenland ice sheet melt
item.dc:creator: Chuncheng Guo, Shuting Yang, Ilana Schiller‐Weiss, Jorge A. Bernales, Steffen M. Olsen, Torben Koenigk, … (+3)
item.description:
Science Advances — matched: ice sheet, Greenland, meltwater, mass loss, overshoot, irreversible, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, sea level, sea-level rise, Earth system model, Earth system, global warming
The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is considered vulnerable to irreversible weakening or collapse under global warming and related Greenland ice sheet (GrIS) melt, yet its resilience to either forcing remains poorly constrained. Here, we use a carbon dioxide emission-driven Earth system model with an interactive GrIS to assess AMOC reversibility under a range of idealized carbon dioxide emission pathways that produce near-linear global warming up to 10 kelvins (K), stabilization across 1.5 to 9 K, and subsequent cooling. We find that although the AMOC reaches threshold-defined collapsed states, these do not represent dynamical tipping in this model: The overturning weakens quasi-linearly with global mean temperature increase yet consistently and promptly recovers under cooling. In contrast, GrIS mass loss accelerates with warming, continues through stabilizations, and is only slowed by cooling, committing the planet to long-term sea level rise. These results reveal contrasting resilience across climate system components: Under transient carbon dioxide forcing, AMOC strength remains dynamically reversible despite continued Greenland meltwater input, whereas the GrIS is locked into persistent decline. Our findings underscore the urgency of rapid emission cuts to limit climate overshoot, AMOC weakening, and irreversible ice sheet loss.

item.title: Rate-induced tipping of ice sheets due to visco-elastic Earth response under idealized conditions
item.dc:creator: Johannes Feldmann, Ann Kristin Klose, Torsten Albrecht, Ricarda Winkelmann
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, grounding line, Antarctic, bifurcation, solid earth, ensemble
Here we examine the tipping dynamics of instability-prone marine ice sheets in interaction with the underlying solid Earth in a simplified model setup. The idealized ensemble simulations allow a systematic investigation of (1) bifurcation-induced and (2) rate-induced ice-sheet tipping for a wide range of representative Antarctic solid-Earth structures. We examine the conditions that lead to shifts in the tipping thresholds, the occurrence of rate-induced tipping or grounding-line overshoots.

item.title: Reduced Evapotranspiration Decreases Land Precipitation Despite Enhanced Moisture Convergence: Insights from Perturbed Parameter Ensembles of Earth System Models
item.dc:creator: Benjamin G. Buchovecky, Francis Hugo Lambert, Claire M. Zarakas, Marysa M. Laguë, Charlie D. Koven, INEZ Y. FUNG, … (+2)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, radiative forcing, ensemble, climate change
Abstract Both canonical theory and climate model simulations predict an increase in globally averaged precipitation with radiatively-forced warming. However, terrestrial processes control surface water and energy fluxes, and therefore can impact surface temperatures independently of radiative forcing. Here, we investigate the sensitivity of the global hydrological cycle to warming induced by changes in land surface conditions using perturbed parameter ensembles from two climate models, which sample a broad range of evapotranspiration (ET) states through modifications to land model parameters. The parameters are perturbed within the range of observationally constrained uncertainty and alter ET through different land surface pathways. We find that reduced ET drives warming yet decreases land-mean precipitation, which we link to strong decreases in near-surface relative humidity from warming. These decreases in relative humidity overcome increases in specific humidity and moisture convergence over land, which are also caused by shifts in large-scale circulation. We explain the tropical precipitation response to ET forcing with a simple scaling that relates changes in the land-ocean contrast in relative humidity to land-mean precipitation change. Further, the suppressed ET induces a shortwave cloud response that amplifies warming. Our results highlight that changes to land surface properties at the magnitude of parametric uncertainty influence warming and precipitation. ET-driven warming reduces land precipitation, opposite in sign to the precipitation increase from radiatively-forced warming. This response is not directly captured by scalings of the global hydrological cycle with radiative forcing. We therefore establish the potential significance of terrestrial ecosystem functioning, and its response to climate change, for hydroclimate.

item.title: Climate Change and the Stability of Glacier-Fed River Systems: Implications for Water Security in Vulnerable Regions
item.dc:creator: Chukwuemeka John
item.category: Journal of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination
item.description:
Journal of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination — matched: glacier, meltwater, mass loss, predictability, climate change
This study examines how climate change is reshaping the stability of glacier fed river systems and the implications for water security in vulnerable regions. Glaciers function as natural water storage, moderating seasonal and interannual variability, yet rising temperatures and altered precipitation regimes are accelerating glacier retreat worldwide. Using an integrated methodological framework combining climate data, glacier mass balance modelling, hydrological simulation, and water security indicators, the study assesses observed and projected changes in river flow magnitude, timing, variability, and extremes across glacier dependent basins. Results show widespread and persistent glacier mass loss, with short term increases in meltwater runoff followed by long term declines in river discharge as ice reserves diminish. Seasonal peak flows are shifting earlier in the year, while late season low flows are becoming more pronounced, reducing flow reliability during periods of high demand. Increased interannual variability and more frequent hydrological extremes further undermine river system stability. These changes translate directly into declining water availability, reduced predictability, and heightened risk for agriculture, hydropower generation, domestic supply, and aquatic ecosystems. The discussion highlights strong spatial differences driven by climatic setting, glacier characteristics, and governance capacity, demonstrating that vulnerability is unevenly distributed across regions. The findings underscore the limitations of water management frameworks based on historical conditions and emphasize the need for adaptive and forward-looking strategies. By explicitly linking cryospheric change to river stability and water security, this study informs climate hydrology research and supports policy planning adaptation.

item.title: Miocene−Pliocene Nenana Gravel deposition in response to tectonic denudation of the Alaska Range (USA)
item.dc:creator: Adrian M. Bender, Richard O. Lease, Lee B. Corbett, Paul Robert Bierman, Brent M. Goehring, Marc W. Caffee
item.description:
Geology — matched: Pliocene, cosmogenic
Disentangling the effects of tectonics and Pliocene−Pleistocene climate forcing on rates of erosion remains key to understanding hypothesized feedbacks among these processes. In central Alaska (United States), deposition of the Nenana Gravel has long been attributed to foreland basin sedimentation coupled to tectonically controlled Miocene−Pliocene Alaska Range exhumation. However, recent cosmogenic burial dating of the lower Nenana Gravel implies that deposition did not begin until ca. 2.3 Ma, consistent with Alaska Range erosion driven by concurrent intensified glaciation during Pleistocene global climate changes. Our new 3.67 ± 0.75 Ma cosmogenic 26Al/10Be isochron burial age at the top of the Nenana Gravel exposed at the Suntrana section indicates that deposition concluded ∼1 m.y. before the previously reported onset. We show that the prior data do not support early Pleistocene burial, but instead yield a 5.5 ± 1.5 Ma simple 26Al/10Be burial age of initial Nenana Gravel deposition, consistent with tephrochronologically constrained 6.7 ± 0.1 Ma strata that conformably underlie the gravel. Deposition of the ∼800-m-thick Nenana Gravel exposed at the Suntrana section thus started between 6.7 ± 0.1 Ma and 5.5 ± 1.5 Ma and concluded by 3.67 ± 0.75 Ma, concurrent with increased Alaska Range exhumation rates associated with tectonic forcing at ca. 7−6 Ma. The Nenana Gravel therefore records Alaska Range denudation induced by Miocene−Pliocene tectonics, and not early Pleistocene climate.

item.title: Differentiating Westerly and Asian monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean since the late Pliocene
item.dc:creator: Yi Yang, Fei Yu, Jingtao Zhao, Xue Ding, Panfeng Li, Shuang Wang, … (+5)
item.description:
Communications Earth & Environment — matched: Pliocene, Earth system model, Earth system
Asian dust flux is a fundamental regulator of global climate and marine biogeochemical cycles, yet it is difficult to separate the dust fractions delivered to the tropical Pacific Ocean by the Westerlies and East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM). We present a 4-million-year record of eolian evolution from the Philippine Sea to deconvolve these two distinct transport systems on the basis of grain-size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting. Our results show that the Westerlies component is primarily derived from hyper-arid deserts, whereas the EAWM-driven component originates from the semi-arid margins of East and Central Asia. Of importance is the finding that Westerly-driven transport reflects a coherent response to global cooling and hemispheric thermal gradients, whilst the Asia monsoon contribution is mediated by vegetation cover. We further demonstrate that hydroclimatic fluctuations in EAWM marginal zones modulate dust availability through vegetation-induced surface roughness and pedogenic refinement, resulting in a pronounced non-linear relationship between dust flux and wind energetics. This suggests the ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus the tropical ocean, necessitating integration of dynamic vegetation impacts and anthropogenic landscape interventions on dust into Earth System Models to predict global carbon cycling in a warming world. “Ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus on the tropical ocean, shown using grain size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting of a 4-million-year-long sediment record from the Philippine Sea”

item.title: 4D sensitivity kernels for infrasound atmospheric propagation: considering the need and impact of time dependent observation operators for acoustic wave observations in data assimilation methods
item.dc:creator: Raphael F. Garcia, Marc Bocquet, Sol\`ene Gerier, Roland Martin
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: data assimilation, ensemble
arXiv:2610.36810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The long range propagation of acoustic waves in Earth's atmosphere is sensitive to winds and temperature variations in the upper atmosphere. Thus, infrasound observations have a strong potential to improve numerical weather models by data assimilation methods. However, because acoustic waves propagate slowly, the atmospheric parameters can change during the propagation of the acoustic waves. This change of atmosphere properties is usually not taken into account by infrasound simulation tools which generally assume stationary atmosphere models. In order to close this modeling gap, we present here a method to compute the linear sensitivities of infrasound observables to atmospheric parameters varying both in space and time. We show that adjoint based methods can easily handle this computation of 4D sensitivity kernels, also called time variable observation operators in the data assimilation community. Then, we discuss the capabilities of various data assimilation methods to handle such observation operators. We demonstrate that only variational methods with data assimilation windows longer than the propagation duration of the long range infrasound can accommodate these observations, as well as their ensemble counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of assimilating such long range infrasound observations, and we quantify the relative impact of linear approximation of observation operators and stationary approximation of the atmosphere model by assimilating propagation time observations of circumnavigating Lamb waves in Lorenz'96 low-order model. The results of this data assimilation experiment demonstrate that the time variability of atmospheric parameters should be taken into account even for infrasound propagation times limited to 2 or 3 time steps of the atmosphere model.

item.title: Geochemical and granulometric fingerprints of 8200 years of westerly wind variability in inner‐fjord lake sediments from Svalbard
item.dc:creator: Zofia Stachowska, Willem G. M. van der Bilt, Jan Kavan, Mark F.A. Furze, Ingunn H. Thorseth, Mateusz Czesław Strzelecki
item.description:
Boreas — matched: Arctic, sea ice, paleoclimate, Holocene, climate dynamics
The Arctic is warming faster than any other region on Earth. As sea ice diminishes, the surface boundary conditions, such as roughness and air–sea coupling, change and open‐water fetch increases. This may enhance wind forcing on Arctic coasts. Lake sediments can record these changes through the deposition of wind‐blown grains and elements, offering insights into past wind and climate dynamics. We reconstruct c . 8200 years of wind and climate variability using laminated sediments from a closed‐basin lake in central Spitsbergen, Svalbard archipelago, High Arctic. By integrating geochemical, visual and granulometric fingerprints within a multiproxy geostatistical framework, we link aeolian minerogenic input to specific catchment sources. Our findings show that iron (Fe)‐rich coarse silt‐sized clasts originate from distinct dolerite outcrops west and northwest of the lake, upwind of the dominant summer westerlies. This reveals a locally filtered westerly input that aligns with valley‐fjord channelling. We identify four phases of enhanced aeolian activity during the Mid‐ and Late Holocene, which occurred when local boundary conditions were favourable for entraining and transporting sediment into the basin. Major shifts in sediment sources and depositional conditions coincide with the end of the Holocene Thermal Maximum and the gradual onset of the Neoglacial. However, the reconstructed wind signal demonstrates a comparatively stable long‐term behaviour, with no clear correspondence to regional palaeoclimate records.

item.title: Contrasting Tropical SST Warming in Two Climate Models: The Roles of Winds, Clouds, Evaporative Cooling, and Ocean Dynamics
item.dc:creator: Minmin Fu, Alexey V. Fedorov
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, Earth system model, Earth system, climate feedback, greenhouse gas
Abstract To investigate why climate models simulate diverse tropical Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) changes under greenhouse-gas forcing, we utilize two configurations of the Community Earth System Model (CESM2) that differ in their atmospheric component (CAM6 and CAM4). Under abrupt CO 2 quadrupling, CAM6 simulates over double the weakening of the east-west equatorial SST gradient compared to CAM4 by end-of-century. To understand this contrast, we conduct overriding experiments that replace wind stress, or wind stress and shortwave fluxes, with values from the preindustrial control experiment. In CAM6, low clouds amplify climate warming and act as a forcing and positive feedback on reductions in the east-west SST gradient. In contrast, in CAM4, low clouds act as a negative climate feedback and provide little contribution to the SST gradient reduction. In both models, interactive wind stress leads to a strong positive feedback (i.e., the Bjerknes feedback). The two models also diverge in their short-term SST responses: CAM6 exhibits an immediate weakening of the zonal SST gradient, while CAM4 initially shows a steepening. Our findings highlight the importance of shortwave radiative and Bjerknes feedbacks, evaporative cooling, and ocean dynamics, all of which control tropical Pacific SST pattern formation.

item.title: High- and low-latitude forcing on precipitation variations over the central Qilian Mountains since 18.5 ka
item.dc:creator: Yun Cai, Jingran Zhang, Liangqing Cheng, Xianqiang Meng, Liang Yi, Hao Long
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: deglaciation, Holocene, proxy, global warming
The moisture of the northeastern Tibetan Plateau is jointly shaped by the East Asian Summer Monsoon (EASM) and the mid-latitude Westerlies, the two key atmospheric circulation systems originating from low- and high-latitudes, respectively. Modern observations demonstrate that the intensity change and meridional position of the Westerlies directly modulate the EASM precipitation, which sustains vast human populations and ecosystems across East Asia. However, the interaction between these two systems over geological time remains controversial, partly due to controversies in the reconstructed past precipitation intensity. Here, we present a high-resolution multi-proxy loess record (ZES) spanning the past 18.5 ka from the central Qilian Mountains, located in the monsoon marginal zone where both systems jointly operate. We first found that loess–paleosol carbonate δ 18 O of ZES record captures a summer signal and covaries inversely with δ 13 C, which tracks monsoon precipitation intensity. Together with comparisons between modern observations and geological records, this constrains EASM-dominated precipitation. We then establish a robust EASM index from multiple independent proxies including magnetic susceptibility, total carbonate content, dolomite content, carbonate δ 13 C, and colour reflectance. Our results reveal that EASM precipitation responded to combined high- and low-latitude forcing on both millennial timescales during the Last Deglaciation and orbital timescales manifested in the long-term trend since 18.5 ka, with the pre-Boreal oscillation offering complementary insights into early-Holocene centennial-scale interactions. The EASM precipitation intensity was suppressed during the Last Deglaciation, strengthened gradually through the early Holocene, peaked from ∼7.5 to 1.8 ka, and subsequently declined. Direct comparison of Westerlies and EASM signals retrieved from the same loess sequence reveals coupled interaction between the two systems since the mid-late Holocene, with westerly intensification accompanying monsoon strengthening. These findings indicate bidirectional linkage between high- and low-latitude systems and further suggest that, under continued global warming, the monsoon marginal zone of northwestern China may experience a progressive increase in precipitation.

item.title: FASST: A Compact Stateless Atmosphere Model for Long-Term Ocean Coupling
item.dc:creator: Pratham Aggarwal, Duncan Watson-Parris, William E. Chapman
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: sea ice, coupled climate model, emulator
arXiv:2610.36297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupled climate simulations are computationally expensive, largely because of the atmosphere. We introduce FASST, a coupled climate model that retains the prognostic POP2 ocean while replacing the atmosphere and sea ice with lightweight U-Net emulators. The atmospheric emulator is diagnostic, predicting surface fluxes from the evolving ocean-ice state every $6$ simulated hours, while the sea-ice emulator advances the ice state monthly. For $140$ years of unforced integration, FASST maintains a stable global-mean climate without SST restoring, with post-transient global-mean SST of $291.30 \pm 0.22\mathrm{K}$ compared with $291.25 \pm 0.10\mathrm{K}$ in CESM$2$ piControl. FASST also captures interannual Ni\~no-$3.4$ variability, although with weaker amplitude than CESM ($0.62\mathrm{K}$ versus $1.02\mathrm{K}$). These results demonstrate that a stateless learned atmosphere can sustain stable, free-running coupled climate simulations over century-scale integrations.

item.title: Impact of Cumulus Parameterization and Cloud Microphysics on WRF Simulation of an Extreme Rainfall Event over Maharashtra, India: A 3 by 3 Factorial Assessment
item.dc:creator: Devesh, Satyam Kumar, Akshay Sunil
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: parameterization
arXiv:2610.36944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating extreme monsoon rainfall over the Konkan coast and Western Ghats remains challenging at 9 km resolution, where convection is partly resolved and partly parameterised. This study evaluates the sensitivity of Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations of the 5-7 July 2026 Maharashtra rainfall event to cumulus and cloud microphysics schemes. Nine simulations employed a 3 x 3 factorial design combining WSM6, WDM6 and Thompson microphysics with Kain-Fritsch, Tiedtke and Grell-Freitas cumulus schemes. Rainfall was evaluated against IMD 0.25-degree gridded observations, with IMERG and ERA5 as additional references. A descriptive factorial decomposition showed that cumulus parameterisation accounted for 97.3% of across-experiment variation in mean rainfall, 88.2% in RMSE and 84.7% in spatial correlation, while microphysics contributed 2.0%, 2.1% and 9.3%, respectively. Kain-Fritsch produced the highest spatial correlations (0.533-0.581) but substantially overestimated rainfall. Tiedtke achieved the smallest mean biases and RMSE, although compensating regional errors concealed a 28-34% rainfall deficit over the Konkan-Ghats belt and substantial underestimation on 7 July. Grell-Freitas showed large wet biases and relatively high RMSE. All nine simulations displaced the event-total rainfall maximum approximately 140-195 km northward. WSM6-Tiedtke achieved the lowest RMSE, whereas Thompson-Kain-Fritsch better represented the rainfall spatial pattern. The findings demonstrate that, for this event and fixed model configuration, cumulus parameterisation exerted substantially greater influence on simulated rainfall than cloud microphysics. However, a single-event, single-member experimental design does not establish a universally optimal physics configuration.

item.title: Climate change impacts on the predicted performance of optimized building-integrated photovoltaics
item.dc:creator: Elyas Hannoufa, Eric Johlin
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: climate change, SSP
by Elyas Hannoufa, Eric Johlin Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) are a promising strategy for enhancing building energy performance and reducing carbon emissions. However, most design optimization studies rely on historical climate datasets that may fail to capture the operating conditions buildings will experience under climate change. This study develops a computational framework for the multi-objective optimization of BIPV envelope systems using future climate projections from the CanESM5 model under the SSP3-7.0 scenario. We analyze two system configurations, awning shades and thin-film window coatings, across four cities with diverse climates (Berlin, Los Angeles, Chicago, Singapore), comparing results from conventional EPW files, NASA 2023 historical data, and 2046–2050 climate scenarios. Optimization integrates electricity generation, thermal loads, and daylighting quality to capture building-level trade-offs. Results show that traditional EPW datasets systematically under-predict BIPV performance, particularly in Berlin and Los Angeles. Under 2046–2050 projected conditions, all four cities exhibit performance gains: substantial in Berlin, Chicago and Los Angeles, and marginal in Singapore, with the largest absolute gains in Los Angeles. By 2050, unshaded windows transition to consistently detrimental for building energy balance. Thin-film coatings achieve optimal outcomes at high absorptance, in the 80–90% range, contrary to current low-absorption design practice. Within the CanESM5 SSP3-7.0 scenario examined, these findings show that projected climate conditions can substantially reshape the modeled performance landscape of BIPV systems, emphasizing the need for forward-looking climate projections in building design optimization and the growing importance of BIPV for climate-adaptive and resilient urban buildings.

item.title: Towards operational data-driven regional weather forecasting: extreme-event skill and near-real-time verification with HRRRCast
item.dc:creator: Daniel Abdi, Isidora Jankov, Vanderlei Vargas, Paul Madden, Emily Carpenter, Travis Wilson, … (+6)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: emulator, ensemble
arXiv:2610.36186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving convective-scale skill in data-driven regional weather models requires better representing rare high-impact events, training at native resolution, broadening variable output, and demonstrating performance in real-time settings. Here, we evaluate these challenges using HRRRCast, a data-driven convection-allowing emulator trained on the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analysis data. HRRRCast combines native 3-km training, moderate sigmoid-weighted loss reweighting for reflectivity and precipitation, and broader system improvements including expansion of the training archive from 3 to 9 years (2016--2025), increased vertical resolution, expanded outputs, and architectural upgrades. The weighted loss improves high-threshold skill while preserving common-event behavior. Native-resolution training avoids aliasing from 6-km subsampling and substantially improves fractions skill score at convective scales, with gains that persist across pooling windows. HRRRCast has also been running in near-real-time mode for the past year. In seven months of independent observation-based verification, HRRRCast ensemble means improve several near-surface metrics relative to operational HRRR and maintain strong precipitation and reflectivity performance. Single-member reflectivity skill is strongest at 20--30 dBZ; at 40 dBZ, skill is near parity at 6-km pooling and better at pooling radii $\geq$30 km. Precipitation skill remains competitive through 1 in/h and extends to about 3 in/h in the best recent configuration. A focused comparison with HREF further shows useful low-cost probabilistic guidance for 3-h precipitation. At storm scale, HRRRCast exhibits a displacement--structure trade-off, with generally better storm placement than storm morphology.

item.title: Reconstruction of the 1989 Laguna del Cerro Largo GLOF: an interdisciplinary understanding of GLOF Impacts
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Warner Burton, Frederick Chambers, Lisa C. Kelley, Benjamin Soto Narbona
item.category: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
item.description:
Natural hazards and earth system sciences — matched: sediment core, radiocarbon
Abstract. The March 16, 1989, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) from Laguna del Cerro Largo in Valle Soler, Aysén, Chile, is one of the largest recent moraine-dammed GLOFs in the region. This interdisciplinary approach reconstructs the GLOF downstream impacts using HEC-RAS 2D and GeoClaw from witness accounts. Model results are then validated through field analysis of sediment deposition, dendrogeomorphic surveys, radiocarbon dating. Sediment cores reveal distinct clastic layers attributable to the 1989 event and evidence of an earlier outburst flood from the adjacent Laguna Turbio, dated circa 125 ybp. The model results also indicate a substantially higher peak discharge than official reports, impacting subsequent disaster policy decades later. While dendrogeomorphic sampling was hindered by fungal decay in Nothofagus species, the findings highlight both the potential and limitations of interdisciplinary reconstructions of GLOF events in remote, data-scarce environments.

item.dc:creator: Britta Grusdt, Mahé Perrette, Alexander Robinson
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: ensemble
We provide practical guidelines for producing weighted ensembles of climate models. We distinguish between two approaches, the individual- and the ensemble performance weighting approach, and formulate both in probabilistic terms, making the underlying assumptions transparent. Using constructed examples, we show the advantage of the ensemble weighting approach to account for model co-dependencies and examine how methodological choices affect the climate projections of the weighted ensemble.

item.title: Ensemble-size-dependence of deep-learning post-processing methods that minimize an (un)fair score: motivating examples and a proof-of-concept solution
item.dc:creator: Christopher David Roberts
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ensemble
arXiv:2602.15830v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fair scores reward ensemble forecast members that behave like samples from the same distribution as the verifying observations. They are therefore an attractive choice as loss functions to train data-driven ensemble forecasts or post-processing methods when large training ensembles are either unavailable or computationally prohibitive. The adjusted continuous ranked probability score (aCRPS) is a fair and ensemble-size-unbiased scoring rule when applied to ensembles with forecast members that are interpretable as conditionally independent draws from an underlying predictive distribution. However, distribution-aware post-processing methods that introduce structural dependency between members can violate this assumption, such that aCRPS no longer functions as a fair scoring rule. We demonstrate this effect using two approaches designed to minimize the expected aCRPS of a finite ensemble: (1) a linear member-by-member calibration, which couples members through a common dependency on the sample ensemble mean, and (2) a deep-learning method, which couples members via transformer self-attention across the ensemble dimension. In both cases, the results are sensitive to ensemble size and apparent gains in aCRPS can correspond to systematic unreliability characterized by over-dispersion. We introduce trajectory transformers as a proof-of-concept that ensemble-size independence can be achieved. This approach is an adaptation of the Post-processing Ensembles with Transformers (PoET) framework and applies self-attention over lead time while preserving the conditional independence required by aCRPS. When applied to weekly mean $T_{2m}$ forecasts from the ECMWF subseasonal forecasting system, this approach successfully reduces systematic model biases whilst also improving or maintaining forecast reliability regardless of the ensemble size used in training or real-time forecasts.

item.title: A Comparative Study of Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks for Storm Surge Prediction in Tampa Bay
item.dc:creator: Mandana Farhang Ghahfarokhi, Anahita Farhang Ghahfarokhi, Mahta Zamanizadeh, Seyed Hossein Sonbolestan
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: neural network
arXiv:2408.05797v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we compare the performance of three popular deep learning architectures: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and CNN-LSTM in water level prediction over different time window sizes. We used wind, pressure, and tide data from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) stations. Our results show that the LSTM model generally outperformed the other models in forecasting water level trends. By applying LSTM, we achieved a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.006, making it the most reliable option for real-world use. We predicted water levels using wind, pressure, and tides. Wind, pressure, and tide data are time-based features that lack spatial patterns. Consequently, LSTM performed better than spatial methods, such as CNN. We also investigated Hurricane Ian, which occurred in Tampa Bay in September 2022 and caused a significant storm surge. Our findings show that CNN and CNN-LSTM performed slightly better than LSTMs during powerful storms, such as hurricanes. Hurricanes are seldom observed in training data, and CNN-based models are more reliable when predicting data that were not included in the training. To explain how environmental factors affect the predicted water level, we used the perturbation method. The perturbation shows that the tide is more effective at predicting water levels than wind and pressure. This study demonstrates the potential of deep learning to improve storm surge prediction accuracy.

item.title: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
item.dc:creator: Rebecca G. Topness, Elizabeth K. Thomas, Michaela Fendrock, Gerard A. Otiniano
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: proxy
Lake models are powerful tools for disentangling complex past climate data preserved in sediments. These models can be hard to set-up for lakes that are not well-observed. We improve an existing model with code to simulate water runoff and establish guidelines for setting-up the model when data are scarce. Using our workflow, more scientists can apply this tool to more lakes and gain a better understanding of the climate histories stored in their sediments.

item.title: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking in structured and unstructured grids
item.dc:creator: Ross Vennell, Laurin Steidle, Malcolm Smeaton, Romain Chaput, Ben Knight
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Ocean currents transport everything from pollution to marine larvae, but tracking millions of virtual particles to understand these movements typically requires weeks of computer processing. OceanTracker solves this bottleneck by being over ten times faster than existing tools, completing million-particle simulations in under an hour on standard computers. This speed breakthrough enables scientists to generate heat maps and analyze connectivity patterns between ocean regions.

item.title: Including the triple isotopic composition of dissolved oxygen in the ocean into the iLOVECLIM model (version 1.1.7): development and evaluation
item.dc:creator: Emeline Clermont, Ji-Woong Yang, Thomas Extier, Didier M. Roche
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
The triple isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen (17Δ) is used to reconstruct past global biospheric productivity. We present the first implementation of the oceanic contribution (17Δocean) in the intermediate-complexity model iLOVECLIM. Photosynthesis, respiration, and air–sea gas exchange are represented under preindustrial conditions. Model results agree with observations, providing a future key tool to study marine biogeochemical processes and past ocean biospheric productivity.
